lessons.intro: You will learn why reading notes again feels productive but builds weak memories. Knowing this saves hours of effort that does little good.

cards.b: A second read makes the text feel easy to follow. That ease comes from recognition, not from being able to produce the idea yourself.
In an exam you must pull information out of your head with no prompts. Practising that pull is what strengthens the memory.
Spend most of your study time testing yourself and checking what came back. Re-reading can stay as a short warm-up, not the main activity.

fig.title: Re-reading versus recall
fig.note: Recall and checking do the memory work.

ex.q: You reread a chapter three times and it feels easy. What is the best next step?
o: Close the book and recall it
ex.why: Feeling familiar only means recognition is working. Closing the book and recalling the key ideas tests the memory you will need in an exam.

lessons.tip: If it feels easy to read, it is probably not yet hard enough to remember.

quiz.q: Which activity builds stronger long-term memory?
quiz.why: Pulling an idea out of memory is the act that strengthens it.

quiz.q: Why does re-reading feel productive?
o: Familiar text feels easy to follow
quiz.why: Recognition feels like understanding, which is why it misleads.

lessons.t: Free recall: close the book and write
lessons.intro: You will learn free recall, a simple method where you write everything you remember with no notes. It shows you exactly what is missing.

cards.b: Put the source away and write every idea you can remember on a fresh sheet. Write in whatever order the ideas come to you.
Open the material and compare. Mark what you missed or got wrong in a different colour so the gaps stand out.
Test again on the gaps after a short break. Each round shrinks the list of things you cannot yet recall.

fig.title: Ideas recalled per round
fig.note: Each blank-page round recalls more of the topic.

ex.q: A learner recalls 6 of 10 key points on the first blank-page try. After a second attempt they recall 9. How many points did they gain?
ex.why: The gain is 9 minus 6, which is 3 points. Their missing list shrank from 4 points to 1.

lessons.tip: Write first, check second, because looking before writing hides what you do not know.

quiz.q: What is the first step in free recall?
o: Write from memory with notes away
quiz.why: You must generate the ideas yourself before checking the source.

quiz.q: Why mark gaps in a different colour?
o: It makes the missing ideas easy to spot
quiz.why: Clear marks show exactly which ideas need another round.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to build and use flashcards that force retrieval. Done well, a deck of a few hundred cards can cover a whole course.

cards.b: Make the front a specific question and the back a short answer. Vague prompts let you nod along without really recalling anything.
Commit to an answer out loud or on paper before you check. The effort of committing is the part that does the learning.
Put cards you got right in a later pile and reshuffle the rest. Keep the unknown pile small so you focus on what matters.

fig.title: Card sorting after a pass
fig.note: Reshuffle the highlighted Miss card into the next pass.

ex.q: You have 40 cards. On your first pass you know 28. How many cards go in the unknown pile?
ex.why: Unknown cards are the total minus the known ones, so 40 minus 28 gives 12. Those 12 go into the reshuffled pile for the next pass.

lessons.tip: A flashcard you can answer instantly every time is ready to be spaced out.

quiz.q: Which front side makes a stronger flashcard?
quiz.why: A specific question forces recall, while a single word lets you nod along.

quiz.q: Why commit to an answer before flipping?
o: The effort of retrieving drives learning
quiz.why: Retrieval effort is what strengthens memory, even when the answer turns out to be wrong.

lessons.t: Retrieval practice after a single reading
lessons.intro: You will learn why testing yourself right after a lesson beats reviewing the notes. It turns a short reading into knowledge that lasts.

cards.h: Test while the material is fresh
cards.b: Within minutes of finishing, try to answer three questions from memory. This shows you what actually transferred from the reading.
A wrong attempt followed by the correct answer still helps. The struggle primes your brain to notice the right answer.
Five questions straight after study are enough. Done consistently, this habit beats one long review session.

fig.title: Learning loop after each lesson
fig.note: Attempt before checking, then retry the misses.

ex.q: A student reads a 20-page chapter and then answers 5 questions from memory, getting 3 right. What is the percentage correct?
ex.why: 3 out of 5 is 0.6, which is 60%. The two wrong answers show exactly what to review next.

lessons.tip: Ask yourself a question the moment you finish a page, not after the whole chapter.

quiz.q: When is the best time for a first self-test?
quiz.why: Testing soon after study shows what transferred, and the wrong answers guide revision.

quiz.q: A wrong answer followed by the correct one is:
quiz.why: Struggling to retrieve and then seeing the answer improves later recall.

lessons.t: Explaining ideas in your own words
lessons.intro: You will learn to explain a concept in plain language, as if teaching a friend. This exposes gaps that reading alone hides.

cards.b: Pretend you are teaching someone with no background. Use simple words and define any jargon you need.
Link the new concept to an example from your life or from another subject. Connections give the memory more places to attach.
The point where your explanation breaks down marks the exact gap. Go back to the source for that part, then try again.

fig.title: Vague versus clear explanation
fig.note: Clear explanations name specific inputs and outputs.

ex.q: Which explanation best shows understanding of photosynthesis?
o: Plants turn light, water and carbon dioxide into sugar and oxygen
Plants need the sun to live
ex.why: A strong explanation names the inputs and outputs. Vague phrases like something with light hide what you do not understand.

lessons.tip: If you cannot explain it simply, you do not yet understand it well enough.

quiz.q: What does explaining to a novice reveal?
quiz.why: Stalling or using vague words shows exactly where your understanding is incomplete.

quiz.q: Why link new ideas to familiar examples?
o: To give memory more places to attach
quiz.why: Connections create more retrieval routes, so the idea is easier to find later.

lessons.intro: You will learn to summarise a topic from memory, then spot what is missing. It is a quick way to test your overall grasp of a chapter.

cards.b: Write a summary of the whole topic in about 100 words, with no notes. Aim for structure: a main idea, then key supporting points.
Check your summary against the chapter. Note the main points you left out and any claims that are wrong.
Rewrite the summary including the missed points. The second version tests whether the new ideas have stuck.

fig.title: Blank-page summary method
fig.note: Each loop reveals what the summary still misses.

ex.q: A chapter has 6 key points. Your blank summary includes 4 of them correctly. How many points are missing?
ex.why: Total key points minus the points you included gives the missing count. Six minus four is 2 points to add on the next attempt.

lessons.tip: Write the summary before you open the chapter, even if it feels messy.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a blank-page summary?
o: To check your overall grasp from memory
quiz.why: It tests what you can retrieve, and comparing reveals the gaps.

quiz.q: After comparing, what should you do with the missing points?
o: Add them in a second attempt
quiz.why: Rewriting with the gaps filled tests whether the new information has stuck.

lessons.t: Practice questions before you feel ready
lessons.intro: You will learn why attempting practice questions early beats waiting until you feel prepared. Confidence should follow testing, not come before it.

cards.b: Confidence after reading often runs ahead of actual skill. Learners who wait to feel ready tend to test themselves too late.
Try a question before reading the worked solution. Even a failed attempt makes the explanation stick better.
Start with questions you can nearly do, then increase the difficulty. This keeps the work challenging without being discouraging.

fig.title: Questions attempted so far
fig.note: Attempts add up quickly when you start early.

ex.q: You plan to attempt 3 practice sets a week with 10 questions each. How many questions will you attempt in 4 weeks?
ex.why: Three sets of 10 is 30 questions a week. Over 4 weeks that is 30 times 4, which is 120.

lessons.tip: Attempt the first question today, because starting early beats waiting to feel ready.

quiz.q: Why attempt questions before reading the solution?
o: Trying first makes the solution stick better
quiz.why: Attempting first creates a need for the answer, which improves retention when you see it.

quiz.q: Why start with easier questions?
o: They keep work challenging without discouraging you
quiz.why: Starting near your level builds momentum, and you can then raise the difficulty.

lessons.intro: You will learn the generation effect, the finding that producing an answer yourself beats reading it. You can use it with almost any subject.

cards.b: Before reading a definition, guess it from the context or your own knowledge. Generating the idea primes you to remember the real version.
Cover key terms in your notes and predict them. Blanks force your mind to supply the content rather than skim past it.
Invent a new example of a concept and test whether it fits. Creating examples shows whether you understand the rule or only the wording.

fig.title: Missing-number practice
fig.note: Predict the blank before checking the sequence.

ex.q: A learner covers the word mitochondria in their notes and predicts it from the clue powerhouse of the cell. What does this prediction practice strengthen?
o: Recall of the idea behind the term
ex.why: Predicting forces the mind to produce the term from its meaning. That generation is what strengthens the link.

lessons.tip: Guess first, even when you are unsure, because a wrong guess still primes the right answer.

quiz.q: In the sequence 3, 6, 9, ?, 15, what fills the blank?
quiz.why: The sequence rises by 3 each time, so 9 plus 3 gives 12, and 12 plus 3 gives 15.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of generating answers yourself?
o: It produces stronger memory than reading
It removes the need to review
quiz.why: Producing an answer engages memory more deeply than passively reading it.

lessons.t: Designing recall tests for complex topics
lessons.intro: You will learn how to write your own recall questions for a complex topic. Good questions reveal understanding, not just memory of wording.

cards.b: Questions that start with why or how demand reasoning. Simple what questions often reward recognition instead of understanding.
Break a large topic into smaller linked questions. Answering each part first makes it easier to rebuild the whole topic.
Write a question that applies the idea to a new situation. Transfer to unfamiliar problems is the true mark of learning.

fig.title: Building a recall test
fig.note: Start broad, then narrow to reasoning and transfer.

ex.q: Which question tests understanding best for the topic compound interest?
o: What is the word for interest on interest?
Define compound interest in one word
Name the banks that offer it
Why does compounding grow savings faster than simple interest?
ex.why: A why question needs reasoning about how interest is added to the balance, which shows understanding rather than word recall.

lessons.tip: Write three questions per topic, one each for what, why and apply.

quiz.q: Which question demands the most reasoning?
o: What is the term for X?
Why does method A work when B fails?
quiz.why: Why questions require connecting ideas, so they test understanding instead of recognition.

quiz.q: What makes an application question valuable?
o: It asks you to use the idea in a new situation
quiz.why: Applying a concept to something new shows whether you can transfer what you learned.

lessons.t: The forgetting curve and why it matters
lessons.intro: You will learn why memories fade quickly after learning, and why that fading should shape how you study. Knowing the curve helps you plan your reviews.

cards.b: Ebbinghaus showed in the 1880s that newly learned material is forgotten fast, with much of it lost within a day. The fade continues unless the memory is revisited.
A review just before you would forget strengthens the memory and makes the next fade slower. Timing matters more than total time.
Schedule a quick check a day after learning, then again a few days later. Early reviews are short but protect what you learned.

fig.title: Recall without review
fig.note: Recall drops sharply when nothing revisits it.

ex.q: A student remembers 10 facts on day 0 and 4 on day 1 with no review. How many facts were lost in the first day?
ex.why: 10 minus 4 leaves 6 facts lost. That steep early drop is why a review soon after learning is so valuable.

lessons.tip: Review the day after you learn something, because that is when forgetting is fastest.

quiz.q: Why is a review just before you would forget useful?
o: It strengthens memory and slows the next fade
It replaces the first study session
quiz.why: A review at the right moment reactivates the memory, so it fades more slowly afterwards.

quiz.q: What does the forgetting curve show?
o: New material fades fast without review
quiz.why: Without review, newly learned material drops away quickly.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to space study sessions across days rather than cramming them together. Spreading practice is one of the most reliable ways to remember.

cards.b: Study the same topic in short sessions on different days. The gaps between sessions force retrieval, which strengthens memory.
Twenty to thirty minutes on three separate days beats three hours in one sitting. Frequent contact keeps the topic active.
Come back while recall still takes some effort. If a topic feels effortless, the review adds little.

fig.title: Spaced practice across a week
fig.note: Short sessions spread across days.

ex.q: Plan A is 90 minutes of study on one day. Plan B is 30 minutes on each of three separate days. Both total 90 minutes. How many more days does Plan B spread practice across?
ex.why: Plan B covers three days instead of one, so it spreads practice across two more days for the same total time.

lessons.tip: Three short sessions on separate days usually beat one long session.

quiz.q: Why does spacing help?
o: Gaps force retrieval, which strengthens memory
Gaps mean you forget the topic
quiz.why: Retrieving the topic after a gap is what strengthens the memory.

quiz.q: Which schedule is better spaced?
o: One hour a day for five days
quiz.why: Daily sessions spread the work over several days, which is spacing in action.

lessons.intro: You will learn expanding intervals, where each review comes after a longer gap than the last. This keeps long-term memory strong with fewer total sessions.

cards.b: Review after one day, then after a few days. Early gaps are short because a new memory is most fragile at first.
When you recall easily, double or triple the next gap. Growing intervals match how durable the memory has become.
If you forget, return to a shorter gap. The schedule adapts to where your memory actually is.

fig.title: Expanding review gaps (days)
fig.note: Each gap doubles after a successful recall.

ex.q: You review a topic after 1 day, then 2 days later, then 4 days later. If the pattern doubles, how long is the next gap?
ex.why: The gaps are 1, 2 and 4, so each one doubles. The next gap is 4 times 2, which is 8 days.

lessons.tip: Double the gap after each easy recall, and halve it after a miss.

quiz.q: What does an expanding interval mean?
o: Gaps that get shorter each time
Gaps that get longer after successful recall
quiz.why: Each successful review lets you wait longer before the next one.

quiz.q: After forgetting a topic, what should the next gap be?
quiz.why: A miss shows the memory is weaker, so a shorter gap brings the topic back in time.

lessons.intro: You will learn interleaving, where you mix different types of problems in one session. It feels harder, but it helps you choose the right method.

cards.b: Blocked practice repeats one problem type over and over. Interleaved practice alternates types, so you must decide which method to use.
Deciding which approach fits is a skill that blocked practice skips. Interleaving builds that decision making.
Interleaved sessions feel slower and messier at first. Performance on later tests usually improves more.

fig.title: Blocked versus interleaved
fig.note: Mixing types builds the skill of choosing.

ex.q: A student practises 12 problems: 4 of type A, 4 of type B and 4 of type C. Which order is interleaved?
ex.why: Interleaving alternates the types, so the student must choose the method each time. The other orders keep each type in one block.

lessons.tip: When you finish a block of one type, switch to a different type before the next problem.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of interleaving?
o: Better choice of method on new problems
quiz.why: Choosing between methods trains the skill that exams demand.

quiz.q: Why does interleaving feel harder?
o: You must work out which method applies
quiz.why: Working out which approach fits adds effort, which is part of why it works.

lessons.intro: You will learn the idea of desirable difficulties, where effort that feels hard often improves retention. This helps you stay with challenging practice.

cards.b: Smooth, fluent practice builds a feeling of mastery. That feeling can hide the fact that little has been learned.
Practice that makes you work harder, such as spacing or mixing, often strengthens memory. Look for effort that is hard but still doable.
Judge a method by how well you can recall a week later, not by how it feels today. Delayed tests reveal real retention.

fig.title: Desirable difficulty loop
fig.note: Effort in the middle is what builds lasting memory.

ex.q: Which practice is most likely to show real learning?
o: Recalling a topic a week after studying it
ex.why: A delayed recall test measures what you can keep, while quick re-reading gives a false sense of mastery.

lessons.tip: Judge your study method by how well you remember a week later.

quiz.q: Why can smooth practice be misleading?
o: It can create a feeling of mastery without real learning
quiz.why: Fluency feels like learning, but it may not carry over to a later test.

quiz.q: What kind of difficulty helps memory?
o: Effort that is hard but doable
quiz.why: Challenge that you can still work through strengthens memory without overwhelming you.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to plan a weekly timetable that spaces and mixes your practice. A clear plan removes the guesswork about what to study next.

cards.b: Choose a small set of topics for the week rather than everything at once. A short list keeps each topic active.
Schedule each topic in two separate sessions, spread across the week. Two touchpoints beat one long block.
Set one lighter day to check what you recall, without new material. This consolidates the week's learning.

fig.title: Two-week rotation
fig.note: Each topic returns twice, and a rest day consolidates.

ex.q: You have 3 topics and 7 days. You want each topic in two sessions, plus one rest day. How many study sessions do you schedule?
ex.why: Three topics with two sessions each gives 6 study sessions. The seventh day is the rest day, so the plan has 6 study sessions.

lessons.tip: Put your hardest topic in the earliest slot of the week, while your energy is highest.

quiz.q: Why keep the number of topics small each week?
o: A short list keeps each topic active
quiz.why: Working on a small set keeps each topic recent enough to strengthen.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a rest or review day?
o: To consolidate learning without new material
quiz.why: A lighter day lets the week's learning settle without adding new load.

lessons.intro: You will learn why cramming feels effective but fades fast, while distributed practice lasts. This helps you resist leaving everything until the night before.

cards.b: Cramming works for a test tomorrow because the material is still fresh. Its benefits drop sharply within days.
Spreading the same hours over weeks produces better retention. Each return session reactivates the memory.
Ask how well you would recall the topic in two weeks. If the answer is worryingly low, you have been cramming.

fig.title: Cramming versus spacing
fig.note: Same total hours, very different long-term results.

ex.q: You have 6 hours to learn a topic before an exam in 3 weeks. Which plan follows distributed practice?
o: 6 hours in one day, then nothing
Read it once on the exam morning
ex.why: Two hours a week across three weeks adds up to six hours and spreads practice out, which gives the longest retention.

lessons.tip: Make your study sessions small and frequent rather than large and rare.

quiz.q: Why does cramming fade quickly?
o: Memories built in one session are not reactivated later
quiz.why: Without later reactivation, the memory trail weakens quickly.

quiz.q: Which is the best test of whether you have been cramming?
o: How much you can recall weeks after studying
quiz.why: Recall after a delay reveals what has actually been retained.

lessons.t: Choosing the right gap between sessions
lessons.intro: You will learn how to pick the gap between sessions so that review lands when recall is hard but still possible. Good timing gives the biggest memory gain.

cards.b: Review when you could still recall the answer, but only with effort. That is when a session does the most good.
Answer a few questions and see how many you get right without help. Mostly easy means wait longer, while many misses mean come back sooner.
Hard topics need shorter gaps and easy ones need longer gaps. Give each topic its own schedule rather than one fixed rule.

fig.title: Adjusting the review gap
fig.note: Use a quick score to set the next gap.

ex.q: On a review, you answer 9 of 10 questions correctly. What should you do with the next gap?
o: Skip the test and keep the same gap
ex.why: Almost-perfect recall means the memory is strong, so you can wait longer before reviewing again.

lessons.tip: If a review feels too easy, wait longer next time.

quiz.q: When is the best time for a review?
o: When recall is hard but still possible
quiz.why: That zone of effort produces the strongest strengthening of memory.

quiz.q: A topic has 4 misses out of 10. What should you do?
o: Shorten the gap and review sooner
Switch to a completely new topic
quiz.why: Many misses means the memory is weakening, so return sooner.

lessons.t: Combining spacing and mixing in one plan
lessons.intro: You will learn how to combine spaced and mixed practice in a single study plan. Using both together is more powerful than either one alone.

cards.b: Spacing decides which days you return to a topic. It controls the timing of your review sessions.
Mixing decides the order of problem types within each session. It trains you to pick the right method.
Return to several topics on spaced days, and interleave their problems within each session. Together they cover memory and choice.

fig.title: Combined plan for each session
fig.note: Spacing and mixing work together in one routine.

ex.q: Which session best combines spacing and mixing?
o: Eight problems of topic A on Monday
Problems from topics A, B and C in one session, with A returning three days later
Re-reading all notes once a month
Two hours of topic C in one block
ex.why: Mixing puts several topics or types in one session, and returning a topic after a gap adds spacing. Both features appear in the second option.

lessons.tip: Mix within a session, and space across sessions.

quiz.q: What does spacing control in a plan?
o: The order of problems within a session
The days you return to a topic
quiz.why: Spacing is about the timing of returns across days.

quiz.q: What does mixing control?
o: The type of problems and their order within a session
quiz.why: Mixing decides which problem types appear together, so you must choose between them.

lessons.t: Why immediate feedback speeds up learning
lessons.intro: You will learn why getting the answer straight away helps you learn faster. Delayed feedback lets mistakes take root.

cards.b: A wrong idea left uncorrected can become a habit. Immediate feedback catches it while it is still easy to change.
Look at the answer as soon as you have attempted a question. A few seconds of checking beats days of confusion.

cards.h: Feedback works best on focused tasks
cards.b: Tight, specific tasks give clear feedback. Vague work, such as reading a long chapter, makes it hard to know what went wrong.

fig.title: The fast feedback loop
fig.note: Quick checking stops errors becoming habits.

ex.q: A learner solves a maths question in a practice set, then checks the answer 2 days later. Which change would give better feedback?
o: Check the answer right after attempting it
Check it only at the exam
Check after reading the whole chapter
ex.why: Immediate checking catches the error while the reasoning is still fresh, so it can be corrected before it sets.

lessons.tip: Check each answer as soon as you give it, while the reasoning is still in your head.

quiz.q: Why is an uncorrected error harmful?
o: It can become a habit that is hard to undo
quiz.why: Early mistakes that go unchecked can be repeated until they become automatic.

quiz.q: Feedback works best when tasks are:
quiz.why: Narrow tasks make it clear which step went wrong and what to fix.

lessons.intro: You will learn to treat each mistake as information about what to fix. A wrong answer often tells you more than a right one about your current gaps.

cards.b: Name the type of error: a concept gap, a careless slip, or a misread question. Each type needs a different fix.
A slip is a quick mistake you can avoid next time. A gap means you need to revisit the underlying idea.
Note the error type beside each miss. Over time the pattern shows where your effort should go.

fig.title: Error type tally
fig.note: Count the error types, then target the most frequent.

ex.q: Over 10 mistakes, 6 were misreads and 4 were concept gaps. Which fix should get more of your time first?
o: Concept gaps, because they are fewer
Misreads, because they are the most common
ex.why: Misreads are the most frequent error here, so slowing down to read questions carefully would cut the most mistakes. Pair that with some concept review too.

lessons.tip: Name each mistake before you fix it, because the right fix depends on the type of error.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a slip and a gap?
o: A slip is a quick avoidable error, a gap is missing understanding
A slip is serious, a gap is minor
A gap is always a careless error
quiz.why: Slips can be avoided with care, while gaps need the underlying idea revisited.

quiz.q: Why record the error pattern?
o: To show where effort should go
quiz.why: A pattern shows which weakness repeats most and deserves attention.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to check your answer properly, so you do not simply land on the right one by chance. Good checking confirms the reasoning, not just the final result.

cards.b: Retrace each step of your working. A correct answer reached by luck will not hold up on a new question.
Make a rough estimate first to see whether the answer is in the right range. Estimates catch big mistakes fast.
Solve the question a second way, or substitute your answer back in. Agreement between two methods builds real confidence.

fig.title: Estimate, then exact
fig.note: Round first, then check the exact result is close.

ex.q: A learner estimates 49 times 21 as about 1000, then calculates 49 times 21 as 1029. What does the estimate tell them?
ex.why: Rounding 49 to 50 and 21 to 20 gives 1000, which is close to 1029. The estimate confirms the answer is in the right range.

lessons.tip: Ask whether the answer is sensible before you accept it.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an estimate before exact working?
o: To check the answer is in the right range
To choose the answer at random
quiz.why: A rough estimate quickly catches answers that are far off.

quiz.q: Why solve with a second method?
o: It shows whether two approaches agree
It proves the first method wrong
quiz.why: Agreement between two independent routes is strong evidence the answer is right.

lessons.t: Turning errors into an error log
lessons.intro: You will learn to keep an error log that records each mistake and its fix. Reviewing the log is one of the fastest ways to stop repeating errors.

cards.b: Write the topic, what you answered, the right answer and the reason. Short entries are easier to review often.
Explain the correct method beside the entry, in your own words. This forces the fix into memory rather than just copying it.
Read through recent entries and quiz yourself on them before new practice. Repeated review of your own mistakes is high-value practice.

fig.title: Errors by topic this week
fig.note: The biggest bar needs the next review.

ex.q: An error log shows 6 errors on fractions, 2 on decimals and 4 on percentages. Which topic should you review first?
ex.why: Fractions has the most errors, at 6, so it deserves the most review time first.

lessons.tip: Keep the log short, and review it before you start new practice.

quiz.q: What should an error log entry include?
o: The topic, the wrong answer, the right answer and the reason
quiz.why: Including the reason makes the entry useful for future review.

quiz.q: Why rewrite the correct fix in your own words?
o: It makes the page look fuller
It forces the method into memory
quiz.why: Restating the method in your own words makes it easier to recall next time.

lessons.intro: You will learn to rate your confidence before checking each answer. Comparing confidence with results exposes what you think you know but do not.

cards.b: Before you check, mark how sure you are from 1 to 3. Recording this stops hindsight from hiding your real level.
Wrong answers given with high confidence are the most dangerous. They show a belief that needs urgent correction.
Correct answers marked low confidence show shaky knowledge. Those topics still need practice even though you scored well.

fig.title: Confidence versus result
fig.note: Confident wrong answers need attention first.

ex.q: You were sure about 8 answers and 5 of them were right. What share of your confident answers were wrong?
ex.why: Three of the eight confident answers were wrong. Three divided by eight is 0.375, which is 37.5 percent, a signal to check those beliefs.

lessons.tip: Treat a confident wrong answer as the most valuable mistake to review.

quiz.q: Why rate confidence before checking?
o: To stop hindsight from hiding your real level
quiz.why: Rating before you see the answer gives an honest picture of what you know.

quiz.q: What does a correct answer with low confidence show?
quiz.why: The right answer was probably luck or partial knowledge, so the topic still needs work.

lessons.t: Seeking specific rather than general feedback
lessons.intro: You will learn to ask for feedback that points to exact actions you can take. Vague praise or criticism rarely helps you improve.

cards.b: Comments like good job or needs work do not show what to change. They leave you guessing about the next step.
Ask what one step in your working could be clearer or more accurate. A narrow question gets a usable answer.
Write one action from each comment, such as showing the units in every step. A single clear action is easier to apply.

fig.title: Vague versus specific feedback

pts: Define the term before using it

fig.note: Specific feedback names a step and an action.

ex.q: Which feedback request is most likely to help you improve an essay?
o: Tell me if it is good
What do you think of it?
Which sentence in paragraph two is unclear, and why?
ex.why: A question pointing at a specific sentence, with a reason, gives you something you can act on immediately.

lessons.tip: Ask a question that names one part of the work, not the whole thing.

quiz.q: Why is vague feedback less useful?
o: It does not show what to change
quiz.why: Without specifics you cannot tell what to do differently next time.

quiz.q: How do you turn a comment into progress?
o: Write one concrete action from it
Save it and never read it
quiz.why: A single concrete action is something you can practise and check.

lessons.intro: You will learn to find the pattern behind a set of mistakes, rather than fixing each one separately. Patterns point to a single underlying cause.

cards.b: Sort errors into groups such as sign errors, wrong formula or misread question. Several misses often share one root cause.
A pattern rarely shows from one or two mistakes. Collect five or more before deciding what is repeating.
If many errors come from one wrong formula, relearning that formula removes them all. Work on the cause to get the widest gain.

fig.title: Errors by cause this month
fig.note: Fixing the top cause removes the most errors.

ex.q: Of 12 errors, 7 came from using the wrong formula. What share of the errors does that cause account for?
ex.why: Seven divided by twelve is about 0.583, which rounds to 58 percent. That single cause is the biggest target.

lessons.tip: Count the causes before you decide what to study next.

quiz.q: Why gather at least five errors before judging a pattern?
o: A pattern rarely shows from one or two mistakes
It is the standard exam size
quiz.why: A small set can mislead, while several errors reveal a shared cause.

quiz.q: If many errors share one wrong formula, what should you do?
quiz.why: Relearning the root cause removes many errors at once.

lessons.t: Using worked examples after a miss
lessons.intro: You will learn how to study a worked example after getting a question wrong. A clear model solution shows you the path you missed.

cards.b: After a miss, read a complete worked example of a similar question. Pay attention to the reason behind each step.
Close the example and solve a new question of the same type. This checks whether the method has transferred to you.
Find the exact step where your working diverged. That point is the one to remember and practise.

fig.title: After a missed question
fig.note: The new attempt tests what the example taught.

ex.q: A learner solves 2x + 3 = 11 and writes x = 7. What is the correct value of x?
ex.why: Subtract 3 from both sides to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2 to get x = 4. Check it: 2 times 7 plus 3 is 17, not 11, so 7 is wrong.

lessons.tip: Study the model answer, then close it and solve a fresh question.

quiz.q: Why redo a similar question alone after reading an example?
o: To check whether the method has transferred
To avoid reading the example again
quiz.why: Solving alone tests whether you can apply the method without help.

quiz.q: What is the main value of comparing your work with the model?
o: It removes the need to practise
It reveals the exact step where your working diverged
quiz.why: Locating the divergence shows you precisely what to correct.

lessons.intro: You will learn to judge your own work using clear criteria written before you look at it. Criteria turn a vague sense of quality into a usable check.

cards.b: Decide what a good answer must include, such as definitions, steps and a conclusion. Knowing the target makes checking easier.
Give yourself a simple yes or no on each point rather than an overall feeling. Separate scores show exactly what is missing.
Track the same criteria across attempts. Rising scores on each point show that your skill is growing.

fig.title: Criteria scorecard
fig.note: The highlighted cell shows a missing conclusion.

ex.q: Your answer has 4 criteria and you met 3 of them. What percentage of the criteria did you meet?
ex.why: Three out of four is 0.75, which is 75 percent. The missing criterion tells you exactly what to add next time.

lessons.tip: Write your criteria at the top of the page before you answer.

quiz.q: Why write criteria before starting?
o: To know the target before you check
quiz.why: A clear target makes self-checking objective rather than a vague feeling.

quiz.q: Why score each criterion separately?
o: It gives a single overall score
It shows exactly which points are missing
quiz.why: Separate scores point to the exact part of the answer that needs work.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to ask a useful question when you are stuck, rather than giving up or asking for the whole answer. Better questions get you unstuck faster.

cards.b: Say which step you cannot make and what you already tried. This gives anyone helping you something precise to work on.
Ask which rule applies or why a step works, rather than requesting the final result. Principles transfer to other questions.
Give the problem five focused minutes first. Struggling before getting help is what makes the explanation memorable.

fig.title: Getting unstuck
fig.note: A precise question names the step and what you tried.

ex.q: Which question is most useful when you are stuck on 3(x + 2) = 15?
o: Give me the final value of x
I am stuck after 3(x + 2) = 15. Should I divide both sides by 3 first, or expand?
ex.why: The precise question names the exact step and the two options, so the answer can be targeted. Dividing both sides by 3 first gives x + 2 = 5, so x = 3.

lessons.tip: Before asking for help, write one sentence naming the exact step you are stuck on.

quiz.q: Why ask about the principle rather than the answer?
quiz.why: A rule you understand helps with many questions, not just this one.

quiz.q: How long should you try before asking for help?
o: As soon as you see it
quiz.why: A short focused struggle makes the explanation stick, and it is quick to stop if nothing works.

lessons.intro: You will learn to combine checking, error logs and confidence ratings into one weekly routine. A consistent routine keeps feedback working without extra effort.

cards.b: Mark each attempt immediately and note your confidence. This keeps the feedback loop short and honest.
Once a week, scan the error log and group the causes. Pick the top one or two causes to focus on next week.
Ask for one precise piece of feedback when you can. Turn it into a single action and track whether it works.

fig.title: Weekly feedback routine
fig.note: Repeat weekly and track whether errors fall.

ex.q: Over a week you log 20 errors, and 12 of them come from one cause. What should be your focus for next week?
ex.why: One cause produces 12 of the 20 errors, which is 60 percent. Targeting that cause removes the largest share of mistakes next week.

lessons.tip: Schedule your feedback review in your calendar, because routines fade without a fixed time.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a feedback routine?
quiz.why: A fixed routine turns feedback into a habit rather than something you do occasionally.

quiz.q: Why track whether a chosen fix works?
o: To see whether errors fall and adjust
quiz.why: Checking the result tells you whether to keep the fix or change it.
